title: Projecting Ravens' 53-man roster: Where should a veteran addition be considered? As Baltimore prepares for training camp, we take our best guess at what the final roster will look like following cutdown day on Aug. 30. Jeff Zrebiec

full_text:
The Ravens' wide receiver room has a few question marks behind two-time Pro Bowler Zay Flowers. Charles LeClaire / Imagn Images
When the Baltimore Ravens take the field for their first full-squad practice of training camp Wednesday, there won’t be a ton of roster ambiguity.
Their top two quarterbacks and running backs are in place. Their top six wide receivers, top eight offensive linemen, top five defensive linemen and top four tight ends, cornerbacks and safeties are set. So too is their kicking battery.
Five-plus weeks of training camp, two sets of joint practices and three preseason games have a way of sparking just as many roster questions as answers. Some players surprise, some disappoint. Veterans are added and subtracted. Trades are occasionally made. And there are far too many injuries influencing the roster construction for all 32 teams.
The Ravens have until Aug. 30 to cut their roster from 90 to the requisite 53. Plenty of factors will emerge to impact their decision making. Until then, this is the best guess on what their roster could look like come Aug. 31.
Who makes the cut?: Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley
Long shots: Skylar Thompson, Joe Fagnano
Biggest question: Who gets the practice squad quarterback spot between Thompson and Fagnano? Waiving Diego Pavia last week makes it a two-quarterback race.
Fact to consider: The Ravens have kept more than two quarterbacks on their initial 53-man roster just once in the past five seasons. Team decision makers clearly don’t think it’s a prudent use of roster space.
Outlook: Huntley was re-signed as Jackson’s primary backup after nearly saving the Ravens’ season last year, leading Baltimore to wins over playoff-bound Chicago and Green Bay teams. The Ravens will want at least one quarterback on their practice squad, and that will come down to either the veteran Thompson or the rookie Fagnano. If it comes down to experience, Thompson will get the spot. If the Ravens want a developmental young quarterback, it will be Fagnano.
Who makes the cut?: Derrick Henry, Justice Hill, Rasheen Ali, Adam Randall
Long shot: Dontae McMillan, Elijah Tau-Tolliver
Biggest question: Will the Ravens have space for four backs? If they don’t, Ali and Randall’s battle for the No. 3 role will be one of the more intriguing roster competitions.
Fact to consider: Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle was part of a Bears offensive staff last year that used a two-running back rotation. If that’s the case in Baltimore, the No. 3 role will essentially be a special teams spot. Ali played 55 percent of the team’s special teams snaps last year.
Outlook: Randall was owner Steve Bisciotti’s hand-picked draft selection. Randall has every reason to feel good about his roster chances. Still, keeping four backs isn’t ideal if only two of them have offensive roles. The Ravens cutting a rookie fifth-round pick is far from unprecedented, so it would behoove Randall to embrace special teams and outplay Ali. He needs to show he can be relied on as a pass catcher and in blitz pickup. If he does, it would be much easier for the Ravens to move on from Ali.
Who makes the cut?: Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman, Devontez Walker, Ja’Kobi Lane, Elijah Sarratt, LaJohntay Wester
On the bubble: Dayton Wade, Chris Moore
Long shot: Cornelius Johnson, Xavier Guillory, Cortez Braham Jr., Octavian Smith Jr.
Biggest question: Are the Ravens comfortable enough with their young receivers to not add a veteran? The addition of a Stefon Diggs or Deebo Samuel would likely mean the subtraction of Walker or Wester and limited opportunities for Lane and Sarratt.
Fact to consider : Bateman, Walker and Wester combined for just 25 catches last year. The Ravens are banking on a Bateman bounce-back and young receivers coming of age.
Outlook: If the Ravens don’t add here and also stay healthy, there’s really only one thing to decide. Are they bullish enough on Wester as their punt returner for him to secure a spot? Walker is set to absorb a bigger role, and Lane and Sarratt, third- and fourth-round picks, respectively, will be in the mix. Wester would enter close to lock territory with no summer missteps. Wade has flashed in practices, but he’d have to play awfully well to get in the 53-man mix.
Who makes the cut?: Mark Andrews, Durham Smythe, Matt Hibner, Josh Cuevas
Long shot: Lucas Scott, Ty Pezza
Biggest question: Who out of Hibner and Cuevas will emerge as a bigger part of the offense? There’s probably room for one of Hibner and Cuevas to earn immediate offensive snaps.
Fact to consider: The Ravens have traditionally carried three tight ends and a fullback. They won’t have a fullback this year, so having four true tight ends doesn’t create any ramifications elsewhere.
Outlook: There is not a whole lot of ambiguity here, either. It remains to be seen how Doyle utilizes the two rookie tight ends. However, barring injuries, they’ll be on the 53-man roster and their ability to contribute on special teams will probably impact how much they are relied on come Week 1.
Who makes the cut?: Ronnie Stanley, John Simpson, Ethan Pocic, Vega Ioane, Roger Rosengarten, Emery Jones Jr., Carson Vinson, Danny Pinter, Andrew Vorhees
On the bubble: Jovaughn Gwyn, Corey Bullock, Evan Beerntsen, Hakeem Adeniji
Long shot: Gerad Lichtenhan, Nick Dawkins, Diego Pounds
Biggest question: From purely a roster standpoint, how will the Ravens fill out the last two or three reserve spots? Assuming Pocic is healthy, the starting group and top reserves are mostly set.
Fact to consider : Of the 16 offensive linemen on the roster, eight were added this offseason. The influx of new faces will create plenty of competition.
Outlook: In a perfect world, the Ravens would keep 10 offensive linemen, and they could do that by going with three running backs or five wide receivers. Vinson and Jones will be the reserve tackles, with Jones having the flexibility to move inside. Pinter is the likely backup for Pocic. That would leave one or two spots for Vorhees, a 17-game starter last year; Gwyn, who followed offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford from Atlanta; Bullock, who made last year’s roster and Beerntsen, a rookie seventh-round pick. Gwyn and Vorhees have the edge.
Who makes the cut?: Nnamdi Madubuike, Travis Jones, Calais Campbell, John Jenkins, Broderick Washington Jr., Aeneas Peebles
On the bubble: C.J. Okoye, Rayshaun Benny
Long shot: David Olajiga, Aaron Graves, Dion Wilson Jr.
Biggest question: Can the Ravens count on Madubuike to regain pre-neck injury form? He was placed on the physically unable to perform list on Saturday but is officially cleared to practice.
Fact to consider: Campbell, who turns 40 in September, played a career-low 46 percent of his team’s defensive snaps last season. Defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver has already spoken with Campbell about reducing his workload.
Outlook: Madubuike is the biggest question here, but hardly the only one. Travis Jones is recovering from a pectoral injury. Campbell is dealing with a personal matter . Washington played three games last year and needed Achilles and elbow surgeries. Jenkins is 37. It’s hard to handicap the roster decisions with so much unknown. However, the Ravens kept Washington despite speculation that they’d move on, making him and Jenkins the likely top two reserves. They’d have room for maybe one more, and that competition will probably come down to Peebles, Okoye and Benny. Peebles diversifies the group a little more with his pass-rush ability.
Who makes the cut?: Trey Hendrickson, Mike Green, Tavius Robinson, Zion Young
On the bubble: Adisa Isaac
Long shot: Kaimon Rucker, Ethan Burke
Biggest question: Will the Ravens add another veteran to this mix? General manager Eric DeCosta has done it several times before with pass rushers, and options like Jadeveon Clowney, Kyle Van Noy and Haason Reddick are available.

full_text:
Monroe Freeling has made a good impression on teammates and coaches early in Carolina's training camp. David Jensen / Getty Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Monroe Freeling is being asked to step out of his comfort zone this summer.
On Saturday, that meant singing “Happy Birthday” to Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young, who shares a birthday with the team’s rookie offensive tackle.
“I don’t think I hit any high notes, not this time around,” Freeling said. “I’ll save those for my rookie (talent show) song.”
The Panthers understand there will be highs and lows during training camp for Freeling, a left tackle last fall at Georgia who has moved to the right side while veteran Taylor Moton recovers from a blood clot in his lungs.
While allowing for dips in his learning curve, Panthers players and coaches like how Freeling is approaching the transition.
“He’s communicating with us really well. I think that’s hard to do as a rookie. There’s a bunch of things that come at you when you’re a first-year (player) in the league. It’s a lot different than college,” tight end Tommy Tremble said.
“But he’s taking it in stride, and he’s working his butt off. I can appreciate that. He’s making good plays here and there, so I’m happy for him. He’s on a steady growth, and you love seeing that from a young guy.”
Tremble added that Freeling is a “cool” dude with a sense of humor. An example: Part of the tackle’s job is to relay the down and distance to tight ends, a task that Freeling has taken to the extreme.
“It’s our responsibility as a tackle to do that. But every single time that he’s in, I’ll turn to him and be like, ‘Hey, it’s second-and-10 by the way,’” Freeling said, laughing. “It’s a habit now. At this point, I do it every single play, so it’s ingrained in me. They’ll know the down and distance, I promise you that.”
Freeling was expected to ease into his first training camp before Moton’s health scare. Panthers coach Dave Canales told Freeling he would have preferred to have him earn first-team reps. But with Moton joining left tackle Ikem Ekwonu, who’s coming back from patellar tendon surgery, on the injured list, the Panthers had no choice but to kick Freeling to the right side and throw his development into hurry-up mode.
“I’ve seen great physical ability. I’ve seen his athleticism, length, sheer strength and power. He’s gotten really strong, especially this summer. He spends a lot of time on that,” Canales said. “He’s got all the tools to do an excellent job over there. Now it’s just about getting comfortable on the right side. Getting your sets right, getting your targets right in the run game. And that’s the part that’s been up and down a little bit for him.”
Freeling played both sides as a backup tackle early on at Georgia before settling in at left tackle, where he started 17 games over his final two seasons. Canales has compared switching sides on the offensive line to brushing your teeth opposite-handed, which Freeling agreed was an appropriate analogy.
“If you brush your teeth left-handed for a couple days, you’ll get used to it. And that’s kind of how it is for playing right tackle,” he said. “I’ve gotta just get some reps at it and get used to the hip flexibility and ankle flexibility. I think I’m getting that. This last practice we just had (Sunday), I made some significant progress in my (pass) sets and everything else.”
Freeling is seeing a lot of outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips, the free-agent acquisition who has been lining up on the left side of the defense. Not that Freeling minds.
“I’m all for the smoke. I want the best competition,” he said. “So if I get to line up against him every single day and he’s been a significant pass rusher in the league, it just means I can get better.”
Beginning Tuesday, Freeling will face Phillips and the Panthers’ other pass rushers in full pads. Canales said that should benefit offensive linemen, who will have more surface to strike on shoulder pads than the shells players have been wearing during the acclimation period.
Either way, Freeling is looking forward to putting on the pads for the first time since New Year’s Day, when the Bulldogs fell to Ole Miss in the quarterfinals of the College Football Playoffs.
“I think there’ll be some growing pains,” said Freeling, the No. 19 pick. “But I’m excited to get physical and play some real football.”
Freeling spent the summer working out at Bank of America Stadium alongside right guard Rob Hunt and other players. The 6-7, 325-pound Freeling didn’t gain any weight, but added strength while doing some lifts for the first time. By the end of the summer, he could pump out three reps of front squats with 365 pounds on the bar.
Freeling used some of his free time turning his South End apartment from college dude décor to something more grown-up.
“I have a couch now, a good couch that I can watch movies on. I mounted the TV, got a TV stand. So it looks a lot more homey,” he said. “I’ve been grinding ‘Game of Thrones’ on it. First time watching it.”
During a break Saturday, Freeling hustled home and caught two episodes before returning to the hotel where the rookies and younger players stay during camp ahead of curfew. Other than serenading Young in the offensive meeting room, that was how Freeling celebrated his 22nd birthday.
In college, Freeling’s birthday would fall just before Georgia started camp. So he’s used to it being a low-key day.
But there will be time for fun and games later, including the rookie talent show when he can show off his vocal skills again.
“He’s cool, man. I like him,” Tremble said. “He’s funny, but he’s a hard worker, too. And I like someone who likes football, so it’s been fun playing with him.”

full_text:
Bears wide receiver Luther Burden III came on late in his rookie year and is facing great expectations this season. David Banks / Imagn Images
Training camp is always a time for hope. This time for the Chicago Bears, there’s actual evidence to fuel it.
Coming off a division title, an 11-6 record, a thrilling playoff win over the rival Packers and a crushing overtime playoff loss to the Rams, the Bears are going to be a hot-button topic over the next six weeks. Are they overrated? Will they regress? They can’t have so many late-game comebacks, but what about the close games they didn’t win? They lost too many guys on defense, but what if Caleb Williams takes another leap?
Williams and coach Ben Johnson have provided Bears fans with two pretty big reasons for optimism.
Veterans report to Halas Hall on Tuesday, and the team takes the field Wednesday for the first practices of 2026 training camp, the most highly anticipated Bears camp since at least 2019. Here are 10 storylines we’ll be watching.
In 2009, Jay Cutler was like a rock star in Chicago. That’s nothing like the hype for Williams: Madden NFL 27 cover , winner of a playoff game, architect of incredible comebacks. Now it’s time to see how much he can ascend for an encore. It can be easy to forget how inconsistent Williams and the offense were last summer. Pre-snap penalties marred camp practices. The offense rarely got into a rhythm.
By Week 3, that was old news, and while the passing offense wasn’t perfect — especially in the first half of games — it was one of the best offenses this city has seen, and Williams did things in the fourth quarter no one has seen. In training camp, how smooth will things look? What wrinkles will defensive coordinator Dennis Allen throw at Williams? How will Williams handle the ups and downs that come with hot August practices? How often can the offense sustain drives?
We learned last year that training camp isn’t always a harbinger of what’s to come, but we’ll all be watching to see where Williams has improved and try to project what that can mean in the regular season. As always, the quarterback is storyline No. 1, but finally for Bears fans, it’s for exciting reasons.
We do it every summer. “This player showed some flashes as a rookie, and now with a full NFL offseason, watch out.” Rarely, though, do those players produce as effectively as tight end Colston Loveland and wide receiver Luther Burden III did late last season. From Weeks 14-18, Loveland and Burden both ranked in the top 18 in the league in receiving yards. They ranked 1-2 among rookies in that stretch, both proving to be incredibly difficult to cover.
Johnson set the standard already by saying he’s buying Burden stock. Loveland missed out on a regular spring and summer last year as he recovered from an injury. Burden also missed a bunch of time in training camp. They’re healthy, they’re gifted and they have a coach scheming up ways to get them the ball. How dominant can they be this summer?
The Burden hype has nearly overshadowed Rome Odunze, who seemed prime for that Year 2 breakout before a foot injury last season. He also had five drops, counting the playoffs.
“Without going into details, those are plays he knows he can make, and let’s make them,” wide receivers coach Antwaan Randle-El said in May. “There are different ways that we can make these plays. You go back and you pull that film (from college) and match it up with the plays that he has made in the NFL as it relates to those 50/50 balls or what have you. The one thing you get is that the confidence is restored; let’s go do it from that standpoint.”
Odunze said he has to get acclimated to his “new normal” when it comes to the bone structure in his foot. That will be top of mind if anything looks off, but he had a strong spring and has the skill set to be the No. 1 receiver. There’s a lot of money at stake, too, if he can take off.
After the surprise retirement of center Drew Dalman, general manager Ryan Poles acted quickly to trade for Garrett Bradbury, who played in the Super Bowl in February and has 88 starts in his career. But then there’s second-rounder Logan Jones. The conventional ideal situation is Bradbury holds down the spot formidably and Jones is ready to take over in 2027, but Iowa offensive linemen tend not to need a ton of NFL reps to be ready to go. Can Jones create a legit competition in camp?
This was a storyline a year ago, as Braxton Jones entered what turned into a four-player competition at left tackle. He ultimately won it heading into opening day, only to lose it in Week 4 before returning to injured reserve later in the season. Ozzy Trapilo’s patellar tendon injury reopened the door to Jones, who was the starter throughout OTAs and minicamp. He’s confident, doesn’t have to worry about his ankle and has plenty of starting experience. But he’ll still have to fend off Theo Benedet, Kiran Amegadjie and Jedrick Wills. The Bears would prefer that Jones leave no doubt once the pads come on.
The team that ranked 29th in yards allowed per carry and 21st in sacks per pass attempt returns its starting defensive line. Johnson and Allen have been open about last year’s coaching focusing too much on scheme and not as much on fundamentals. The spring was all about improving the get-off. Will that be enough when the personnel is virtually the same? The Bears are banking on rebound seasons from Dayo Odeyingbo and Grady Jarrett, and maybe a contract-year-breakthrough for Gervon Dexter. Montez Sweat has often looked dominant in camp. If Poles isn’t seeing what he hoped for up front, does he make a move for more pass-rush help before the season starts?
After parting ways with Tremaine Edmunds, the Bears increased team speed with the addition of Devin Bush, who’s coming off a career year in Cleveland. He’ll be paired with T.J. Edwards, who had to deal with several injuries last season and is starting camp on the non-football injury list. Who steps up in Edmunds’ place, and who wins the reserve roles? Jack Sanborn is back; can he compete with D’Marco Jackson for the No. 3 job? When will Noah Sewell be healthy?  We didn’t see rookie Keyshaun Elliott in OTAs and minicamp, and, like Sewell, he’s on the physically-unable-to-perform (PUP) list to begin camp. Can he get healthy in enough time to work his way up the depth chart? Ruben Hyppolite barely played as a rookie because of injury, those in front of him, and not proving enough on special teams. Is he on the roster bubble?
In a perfect world, the Bears benefit from having the same starting trio at corner as they had in 2023 — Jaylon Johnson, Tyrique Stevenson and Kyler Gordon. But Gordon missed most of the spring practices with yet another injury, and now he’s starting training camp on the PUP list. He played only three games last year but was everywhere in the playoff loss to the Rams. Availability is his biggest issue. Johnson was out all summer. With a fully healthy offseason, will he look like his All-Pro self? It’s a contract year for Stevenson and oft-injured reserve Terell Smith, while rookie Malik Muhammad won’t shy away from getting in the mix.
In the 2026 Bears fan survey, safeties Kevin Byard and Jaquan Brisker didn’t poll as well as I thought in the “which departing veterans will you miss most” category. Part of that might be the ability for fans to quickly move on when the replacements are veteran Coby Bryant and first-round rookie Dillon Thieneman. Reviews were quite positive for Bryant in the spring, and Thieneman had everything the Bears wanted in a first-round pick. Watching them take on the Bears offense will be a fun matchup in camp, and we should get glimpses of how impactful they can be.
Luke Elkin is the most experienced long snapper on the Bears’ roster. That experience is a whopping nine preseason snaps last year when he was an undrafted rookie. He did play with punter Tory Taylor at Iowa and had all of the offseason under Richard Hightower’s tutelage, but he’s…

full_text:
New coaches, quarterback competitions and championship pursuits are among the storylines taking center stage as NFL training camps begin across the league. Illustration: Kelsea Petersen/ The Athletic; Camden Hall / Getty, Aron Sprecher / Getty, Caleb Bowlin / Getty, David Berding / Getty, Kevin Sabitus / Getty
At long last, training camp season has arrived.
The Arizona Cardinals and Carolina Panthers kicked off the action last week because they’ll face each other in the Hall of Fame Game. Meanwhile, the remaining 30 teams will have all opened camp by the middle of this week. Day by day, week by week, the march towards the regular season will unfold at a rapid pace.
From head coaching debuts to new arrivals, to comeback quests, position battles and more, the storylines abound across the league. Here are 10 to follow as training camps get underway.
Thirteen years ago, the Seattle Seahawks followed up the first Super Bowl victory in franchise history with a march that saw them return to the big game only to fall painfully shy of a repeat victory . Champs again, the Seahawks embark on a journey they hope will result in another Super Bowl run.
Repeats are rare. Only eight teams have achieved such a feat. To give themselves a chance, Mike Macdonald and his team have several challenges to overcome. Gone is offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak. In his place: first-year play caller Brian Fleury (previously the San Francisco 49ers’ tight ends coach). Also departed: key veterans such as Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III (Kansas City Chiefs), cornerback Riq Woolen (Philadelphia Eagles), pass rusher Boye Mafe (Cincinnati Bengals), safety Coby Bryant (Chicago Bears). This week, the Seahawks will continue the work of filling the shoes left behind.
Five seasons ago, the Los Angeles Rams became only the second team in NFL history to win a Super Bowl in their home stadium. This February, the Rams hope to repeat that accomplishment as SoFi Stadium again hosts the Super Bowl. Rams general manager Les Snead had a busy offseason, trading for the NFL’s single-season sack leader , Myles Garrett. That blockbuster move came after Snead traded for All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie and further overhauled his secondary by signing cornerback Jaylen Watson, who, like McDuffie, helped the Chiefs win two Super Bowls.
Coach Sean McVay already has a potent offense led by quarterback Matthew Stafford, wide receivers Davante Adams and Puka Nacua and running backs Kyren Williams and Blake Corum. Now, they figure to have one of the more dominant defenses in the league. The Rams will work to put it all together, and as they do, eyes remain peeled for Aaron Donald, who reportedly is considering coming out of retirement to make another run at the Lombardi Trophy.
This offseason saw 10 teams hire new head coaches. Those coaches — Mike LaFleur (Cardinals), Kevin Stefanski (Atlanta Falcons), Jesse Minter (Baltimore Ravens), Joe Brady (Buffalo Bills), Todd Monken (Cleveland Browns), Klint Kubiak (Las Vegas Raiders), Jeff Hafley (Miami Dolphins), John Harbaugh (New York Giants), Mike McCarthy (Pittsburgh Steelers) and Robert Saleh (Tennessee Titans) — all got to work in the offseason while directing voluntary workouts and mandatory minicamps. But now, they really will dive into building, developing and assessing talent and preparing their teams for the opening of the season, which looms just five weeks away.
The offseason featured plenty of comings and goings, and OTAs and minicamps served as an introductory period for some of the biggest names that changed addresses. But now it gets real as the highly coveted stars begin making their presence felt around their new teammates. Some prominent stars found themselves on the move, and they bring to their new teams unique skill sets and lofty expectations.
With the New England Patriots, wide receiver A.J. Brown hopes a fresh start and reunion with Mike Vrabel translate into more bountiful playmaking opportunities than he received in Philadelphia, and the Patriots hope the wideout’s presence translates into more growth for Drake Maye and explosiveness for their offense.
The Denver Broncos hope wide receiver Jaylen Waddle — acquired from Miami — will have a similar impact for Bo Nix and their offense. In Baltimore, the Ravens hope their investment in Trey Hendrickson helps their defense take a leap forward.
Down in Miami, Malik Willis aims to leap from promising backup to franchise quarterback after his departure from the Green Bay Packers. And in San Francisco, Mike Evans will work to further immerse himself in the 49ers offense after 12 seasons with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, where he recorded 11 1,000-yard campaigns and earned Pro Bowl honors six times.
Several teams hope training camp brings with it the healthy returns of some of their biggest stars. In Kansas City, Patrick Mahomes has had a smooth recovery from surgery to repair the torn ACL and LCL in his left knee, and coach Andy Reid told reporters Friday that he’s been cleared to participate in training camp. In Indianapolis, the Colts hope Daniel Jones can pick up where he left off before a ruptured Achilles tendon ended his 2025 revival campaign. Jones, who re-signed with the team this offseason, is expected to be ready to go Week 1.
The Washington Commanders’ 2025 hopes of returning to the NFC Championship Game crumbled as star quarterback Jayden Daniels landed on the injured list. Daniels is now fully healthy and primed to direct a new offense under first-year play caller David Blough. The 49ers endured an injury-plagued 2025 campaign, and defensive end Nick Bosa (ACL) and linebacker Fred Warner (dislocated and fractured ankle) ranked among the biggest losses. San Francisco anticipates having both star defenders back on the field for Week 1, however.
In New York, the Giants face some uncertainty when it comes to star wide receiver Malik Nabers, who tore his ACL in Week 4, had surgery a month later and this spring had to have another procedure. Coach John Harbaugh has declined to make predictions on Nabers’ return, but he won’t open camp on the physically unable to perform list , an encouraging sign. And count the Packers among teams waiting anxiously for good news about their recovering star. Linebacker Micah Parsons tore an ACL and meniscus in Week 15 and continues his recovery, but is expected to open camp on the PUP list. Parsons will spend camp continuing his rehab in hopes of returning at some point midway through the season.
Five NFL teams anticipate quarterback competitions during training camp. The Cardinals, Falcons, Browns, Raiders and Minnesota Vikings all have some sorting out to do at the most important position on the field. In Arizona, Jacoby Brissett, who started 11 games last season, faces competition from journeyman Gardner Minshew and rookie Carson Beck. Brissett missed most of the offseason program while holding out for a new contract. That enabled Minshew and Beck to get more reps than they normally would. Now, with Brissett agreeing Sunday to a restructured contract , LaFleur must decide between the three, although Brissett should be considered the heavy favorite.
In Atlanta, new head coach Kevin Stefanski inherits 2024 first-round pick Michael Penix Jr., who is coming off a torn ACL suffered in Week 11 and returns to face a challenger in Tua Tagovailoa, who signed with the Falcons in free agency following his release in Miami. The pair of left-handed quarterbacks are expected to duke it out throughout camp and the preseason.
Cleveland head coach Todd Monken also inherited a team with an unsettled quarterback situation. Shedeur Sanders started the final seven games of last season, but veteran Deshaun Watson has returned from the Achilles tendon tear that cost him the entire 2025 season. Watson and Sanders are expected to split snaps in camp after doing so for much of OTAs.

title: Top Cowboys training camp storylines: How much better will their defense really be? Jon Machota
summary:
Dak Prescott has yet to get past the divisional round in the playoffs as the Cowboys' quarterback. Chris Jones / Imagn Images
Entering his 11th season, Dak Prescott is extremely aware of the expectations surrounding the Dallas Cowboys. He’s been on four teams that have won at least 12 games during the regular season. None have gotten beyond the divisional round of the playoffs.
The deep postseason run has eluded him and the franchise.
Just making the playoffs would be a big step for the Cowboys
full_text:
Dak Prescott has yet to get past the divisional round in the playoffs as the Cowboys' quarterback. Chris Jones / Imagn Images
Entering his 11th season, Dak Prescott is extremely aware of the expectations surrounding the Dallas Cowboys. He’s been on four teams that have won at least 12 games during the regular season. None have gotten beyond the divisional round of the playoffs.
The deep postseason run has eluded him and the franchise.
Just making the playoffs would be a big step for the Cowboys after winning only seven games each of the last two seasons.
Prescott, however, embraces Super Bowl-or-bust expectations.
“That’s always been my mindset,” he said. “That’s one thing I truly love about the Cowboys organization and the fan base is that it’s that or nothing. That’s what being a competitor is. If that’s not how you’re wired or if that’s not how you think, whether you’re a fan, whether you’re a player, whether you’re a coach, then I think you’re in the wrong business. And honestly, I don’t want you on my team. I love those expectations.”
And he “absolutely” believes they are more realistic this season.
Because of the upgrades made to what was arguably the worst defense in franchise history. That began with hiring first-time defensive coordinator Christian Parker and continued with the veteran additions of outside linebacker Rashan Gary, safety Jalen Thompson, cornerback Cobie Durant and linebacker Dee Winters. They then used first-round picks on do-everything defensive back Caleb Downs and edge rusher Malachi Lawrence.
Dallas also returns almost all of last year’s offense that was one of the NFL’s best.
Beginning this week, the Cowboys will start to see if they’ve done enough to get back into the playoff mix, and perhaps make that deep playoff run that has been missing for the last 30 years.
The Cowboys travel to Southern California on Monday to begin four weeks of training camp practices in Oxnard. To get you ready, here are the five biggest topics entering camp.
There were no fully-padded practices or tackling in organized team activities or minicamp. That changes in training camp. What will Parker’s new defense look like, moving from a 4-3 to a 3-4 base? They will have their hands full with a very talented offense.
“They’re playing with a lot of confidence,” Prescott said a month ago. “You can just tell by the way they’re communicating, whether it’s in walk-throughs, whether it’s there at practice, 7-on-7, guys are taking ownership of what they’re being asked. We’ve got great energy from not only (Parker), but the rest of the coaches. It’ll be a battle. They’ve already gotten us on some of these days in OTAs and the rush isn’t even there. Once you let Quinnen (Williams) and Gary and Kenny (Clark) and all those guys take off and put pressure on me, I’m sure it’s going to be tougher.
“But it’s iron sharpens iron. And super, super excited about it. A couple of those guys have already warned me that it won’t be as easy as last year or as I’ve had in the past. Even that trash-talking or fire-starting is awesome.”
The expectations haven’t been this high for a rookie Dallas defender since at least Micah Parsons in 2021, and it might even go back to Morris Claiborne in 2012 or DeMarcus Ware in 2005.
Downs is expected to make an immediate impact at the nickel cornerback position and safety. He could be near the line of scrimmage, possibly blitzing, on one play and back deep on the next. However he’s utilized, any play the No. 11 pick makes will only feed the hype.
“He’s as advertised,” Parker said last month. “We spent significant time with him before the draft process, so we had a good feel on who he was and knew some people at Ohio State, at Alabama, in terms of how he was on the day to day that we maybe didn’t see in that 30-visit or at the combine.
“He’s been doing great. He’s a worker. He looks for coaching. He craves that. He wants to be corrected. He wants more information. And he works as hard as he can with the extras and everything else. So it’s been good. He’s been good to work with, and I think that he’s trying to advance at the right rate.”
The Cowboys want Guyton to be their starting left tackle. That’s why they used a first-round pick on him two years ago. However, he has underwhelmed, leading to a competition with swing tackle Nate Thomas. If neither can handle starting responsibilities, Dallas could turn to moving All-Pro left guard Tyler Smith out to left tackle. Everyone involved would like to avoid that move, one that would weaken an interior that should be a significant team strength.
“I got to come to work every day and get better,” Guyton said. “There’s obviously competition everywhere on the team. It’s a football team and everyone wants to play, so friendly competition isn’t bad. It brings the best out of people.”
Guyton called his first two seasons a “learning experience.” He has spent the offseason improving his overall strength.
“Coming into the league I had a lot to learn,” he said. “I feel like I’ve learned. I’ve gotten stronger. I’ve gotten better at football. I’m learning more techniques and things like that, so it’s just a learning process. I’m going to continue to try to advance during this (upcoming) season.”
If the defense can be at least respectable, this should be a playoff team. Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, Javonte Williams, Jake Ferguson, Ryan Flournoy, KaVontae Turpin and Brevyn Spann-Ford are more than enough weapons to put up 28-30 points per game. Is there a way they could be even better than last year’s group that averaged 27.7 points per game?
An important piece could be Jaydon Blue. Dallas drafted the former Texas running back in the fifth round last year. While his skill set is the perfect complement to Williams, Blue didn’t come close to having the expected impact, playing in only five games. The Cowboys didn’t do anything in the offseason to upgrade the position, hoping that Year 2 will be a breakout season for Blue.
“I didn’t start off like I should have,” Blue said. “Maybe if it was not practicing the right way or just on a maturity level, I think I wasn’t really there. But just learning from all the vets, having the offseason that I’ve had, I think I’m ready to go.
“Just looking back on the things I didn’t do too well and some of the reasons I wasn’t on the field last year, taking the stuff my coaches were saying and making sure I apply them, whether that’s this offseason or when I’m by myself. … I think I made a 180 from where I was last year. I think I’ve gotten a lot better, whether that’s the football part, the physical part, my body, I feel really good. I’m just ready to go.”
That’s usually a lot to ask for from the Cowboys. However, they have had a very under-the-radar offseason, starting with Pickens signing the franchise tag and showing up to minicamp. Last year, the biggest storyline entering camp was Parsons’ contract situation. Dallas currently doesn’t have any of that drama lingering. Can it stay that way? Could training camp 2026 be all about what is happening on the field?
“Obviously we’re used to it,” Prescott said in June of the offseason drama. “So, it wouldn’t be absurd to have it. But it is good that we won’t have that this year. George is going to be there. I wish he would get the long-term contract, but I’m sure that’s all being talked about and discussed behind closed doors. And it (doesn’t) necessarily (have) to happen immediately. Hopefully these are the last of those questions and we can get him on some long-term (contract) whenever it’s right.
“I just think the focus is in the right place.”

Happy football season, everyone.
Training camp in Green Bay officially kicks off Wednesday with the Packers’ first open practice at Ray Nitschke Field.

full_text:
Micah Parsons continues to work his way back from an ACL tear suffered in December. John Fisher / Getty Images
Happy football season, everyone.
Training camp in Green Bay officially kicks off Wednesday with the Packers’ first open practice at Ray Nitschke Field.
This felt like a rather mundane offseason around these parts. There weren’t any ground-breaking moves — it’s hard to match the Micah Parsons trade from last year — and there might be apathy among fans who are tired of both the No. 7 seed and watching freshly extended Matt LaFleur as head coach. Can you blame them?
Nonetheless, the start of a new season in Titletown is reason enough for optimism, no matter how dreary the outlook without Parsons might be as he recovers from last December’s torn ACL.
Lather on that sunscreen and let’s dive into 10 pressing questions surrounding the Packers entering camp.
The Packers’ best player tore his ACL on Dec. 14 in Denver and underwent surgery Dec. 29. He also got his meniscus fixed, so it wasn’t a clean ACL tear. The Packers have a strict rule of nine months without any football activity for players rehabbing major injuries like Parsons’, so the best-case scenario is he returns to practice on Wednesday, Sept. 30, before that Sunday’s Week 4 visit to Tampa Bay. Assuming he needs a couple weeks before playing in a game, perhaps he returns in Week 5 against the Chicago Bears at Lambeau Field or Week 6 against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football in Green Bay. When speaking this offseason, Parsons preached patience and a long-term outlook instead of the need to rush back.
The three other big names who suffered season-ending injuries last year were tight end Tucker Kraft, defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt and right tackle Zach Tom. Kraft tore his ACL in Week 9, Wyatt suffered a broken fibula and torn ankle ligaments in Week 13 and Tom partially tore his patellar tendon in Week 15. According to recovery timelines given by them at various points this offseason, all should be ready for Week 1 and Wyatt and Tom should be ready for practice on Wednesday. There’s a chance Kraft suits up then, too, but he said at his youth camp recently that we’ll find out if he’s practicing when we show up to the field.
Kraft should be the answer here as the 2023 third-round pick enters a contract year. Wide receivers Christian Watson and Jayden Reed and Wyatt have already been taken care of this offseason. Kraft, who turns 26 in November, might reset the tight end market currently topped by George Kittle’s $19.1 million average annual salary. When he went down last season, Kraft thought he was the NFL’s best tight end. From Weeks 1-8 last season, Kraft ranked third among tight ends in receiving yards, second in touchdown catches and first in yards after catch per reception. He’s also a rock-solid blocker. The only question is not whether the Packers extend him, but when they do — before he steps on the field or after he shows he hasn’t lost a step after injury?
Last Thursday, the Brown County District Attorney’s Office told The Athletic in an email that the investigation into running back Josh Jacobs was still open and that there will be an update provided once a resolution is reached. Jacobs was arrested by the Hobart/Lawrence Police Department in Wisconsin and jailed in late May on five charges relating to domestic abuse. Before appearing in court the next day, Jacobs was released, with the D.A.’s office announcing that there was insufficient evidence to pursue criminal charges at the time and that they had reason to believe there may be additional evidence that would impact what/if criminal charges were appropriate. Jacobs practiced all offseason while under investigation and teammates strongly supported him. There’s no telling when this will wrap up or what the resolution will be.
The Packers’ quest for long-term kicker consistency post-Mason Crosby enters its fourth season. The team has cycled through myriad kickers since moving on from Crosby after the 2022 season — he had spent 16 years in the role — and that group primarily includes rookie Anders Carlson in 2023, rookie Brayden Narveson in 2024 and veteran Brandon McManus over the last two seasons. After the Packers released McManus this spring, it’s up to rookie sixth-round pick Trey Smack out of Florida to improve Wisconsin’s overall mental health.
Regardless of whether Jacobs is on the team, it’s paramount for the Packers that running back MarShawn Lloyd stays on the field. The promising 2024 third-round pick has played in just one game over his two NFL seasons due to a litany of injuries. Running backs coach Ben Sirmans said this offseason that they’re optimistic about Lloyd, whose shiftiness and explosiveness are unlike what any of the team’s other running backs offer, but added that they’ve been optimistic before about the 25-year-old. Lloyd spent months early this offseason trying to solve his body’s problems at a facility in California with Dr. John Meyer, which was detailed in our story here .
We can debate Jordan Love’s place in the NFL quarterback hierarchy all we want, but none of that conversation matters if he’s always on his back. Keeping him upright, which can allow him to be a top-five quarterback in the league, is dependent on the performance of someone who’s never played meaningful snaps on Love’s blind side. The Packers drafted Jordan Morgan in the first round two years ago and the college left tackle at Arizona said he wanted to prove he could play there in the NFL. After cycling between left guard, right guard, right tackle and the bench the last two seasons, Morgan is finally getting his chance to walk the walk and not just talk the talk. The Packers’ offensive success might hinge on whether he can.
According to TruMedia, Packers’ 2025 first-round pick Matthew Golden ranked tied for 85th among wideouts last season with 44 targets, tied for 84th with 29 catches and 78th with 361 receiving yards. He didn’t score a touchdown until the playoffs. While flashes of talent were there, they never materialized into consistent production. After the offseason departures of Romeo Doubs in free agency to the New England Patriots and Dontayvion Wicks via trade to the Philadelphia Eagles, Golden should see many more passes. Both Watson and Reed expressed optimism this offseason about Golden’s immediate future based on what they’d seen from him since last season ended — improved confidence and knowledge of the offense entering Year 2 — with Reed saying, “he’s going to be dangerous for this offense.”
The Packers’ last two first-round cornerbacks, Jaire Alexander and Eric Stokes, didn’t start immediately. Brandon Cisse wasn’t a first-rounder this year, but he was the Packers’ first pick at No. 52. After what appeared to be an underwhelming second half of last season from Green Bay’s cornerbacks despite general manager Brian Gutekunst’s offseason vote of confidence for them, it’s only to natural to wonder how hot, say, Carrington Valentine’s seat might get if he struggles and Cisse impresses. And sorry, fans, Keisean Nixon’s starting spot is likely not in jeopardy because of the fellow South Carolina Gamecock.
While the offense’s success could hinge in part on the play of Green Bay’s 2024 first-round pick (Morgan), the defense’s early-season success might hinge largely on the play of the team’s first-round selection from the year prior. If Parsons misses the first month and a half of the season, Lukas Van Ness is unquestionably the guy on the edge with a host of unproven young guys behind him who will also need to step up — Brenton Cox Jr., Barryn Sorrell, Collin Oliver and Dani Dennis-Sutton. Van Ness will be charged with leading that group and appeared to be hitting his stride early last season before a foot injury that took far longer to heal than expected derailed his progress. With concerns at cornerback and on the edge to start the season, Van Ness can ease the worries of fans and perhaps even the team by…

title: From Daniel Jones to Josh Downs: Which Colts have the most on the line this season? Jones is trying to prove he's the Colts' future at QB. Sauce Gardner is trying to prove he's worth the high cost Indy paid to acquire him. James Boyd
summary:
Can Daniel Jones prove to be the Indianapolis Colts' long-term answer at quarterback? Mykal McEldowney / Imagn Images
Chris Ballard knows what’s at stake when training camp begins Wednesday. The Colts general manager is entering his 10th year in Indianapolis, and for the first time during his tenure, he’s reached the last year of his deal without an extension. Missing the playoffs for the sixth straight year could mean he won’t return for an 11th season. Coach Shane Steichen isn’t safe either. H
full_text:
Can Daniel Jones prove to be the Indianapolis Colts' long-term answer at quarterback? Mykal McEldowney / Imagn Images
Chris Ballard knows what’s at stake when training camp begins Wednesday. The Colts general manager is entering his 10th year in Indianapolis, and for the first time during his tenure, he’s reached the last year of his deal without an extension. Missing the playoffs for the sixth straight year could mean he won’t return for an 11th season. Coach Shane Steichen isn’t safe either. He’s beginning his fourth season at the helm, and without a postseason berth on his resume, he could follow Ballard out the door as the organization pivots to a reset.
Despite the underwhelming results during their stewardship, Colts principal owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon retained Ballard and Steichen and insisted that the team’s sense of urgency “has never been higher.” That pressure, however, isn’t reserved for just the GM and coach. The players must prove themselves, too.
Excluding rookies and second-year pros like Justin Walley and Hunter Wohler, who didn’t play last year due to injury, here are the top seven Colts who have the most on the line in 2026.
Jones is on track to start in Week 1, which would be about nine months after he suffered a season-ending torn right Achilles tendon that derailed his resurgent 2025 campaign. Jones was playing arguably the best football of his career through the first half of last season, and the Colts believed so much in that healthy version of Jones that they rewarded him this offseason with a two-year, $88 million deal to remain in Indy. Now, he must prove last year wasn’t a mirage and that he can be the Colts’ long-term answer at QB.
But if Jones flames out, or worse, gets injured again, it would raise serious questions about his status going forward. While it wouldn’t be cheap, the Colts could cut ties with him if he struggles in 2026, especially if Ballard and Steichen are ousted. The Colts would create $11.6 million in cap space while taking on $35.2 million in dead money if they released Jones after this season. That may seem like a lot of money, but keep in mind that a new general manager would likely consider that the cost of doing business if they don’t want to inherit a mediocre and/or injury-prone QB.
The Colts traded two first-round picks and wide receiver AD Mitchell to the New York Jets in exchange for Gardner last year. It was a bold move for a team that, at the time, sat near the top in the AFC standings, but after Indianapolis lost its last seven games amid a slew of injuries, including a calf injury that sidelined Gardner, the deal that brought him to Indy has faced even more scrutiny. Before the draft, Gardner joked that he was Indy’s first-round pick this year, but this is no laughing matter. The Colts need Gardner, a two-time first-team All-Pro, to return to playing at an elite level. If he does not, Indy could be feeling negative ripple effects of his acquisition for years to come.
Ballard called Latu “the best f—ing rusher in the draft” when the Colts selected him 15th in 2024. But since joining the NFL ranks, Latu has yet to morph into the game-wrecker Ballard envisioned. Last year, Latu took a significant step forward with career-highs of 12 tackles for loss and 8.5 sacks. He even had three interceptions, the second-most on the team. But for the Colts’ defense to reach its ceiling, it needs Latu to turn his flashes of potential into sustained production.
The Colts haven’t had a player record at least 10 sacks in one season since Justin Houston in 2019. It’s Latu’s job to end that drought in 2026. It’s worth noting that Latu also has some financial incentive this season, as he becomes eligible to sign a contract extension at the end of the season.
Ward has been candid about his struggles on and off the field during his brief Colts tenure. After inking a three-year, $54 million contract to join Indy last year, Ward suffered three concussions in his first season and openly contemplated retirement. He’s also discussed the grief he still feels following the death of his 1-year-old daughter, Amani Joy, in Oct 2024. Ward said in the spring that he’s in a better mental space regarding his daughter. He still acknowledged, however, that he can’t control concussions and if he suffers another one, he might walk away from the game.
Downs’ situation is simple as he enters a contract year: The better he plays, the better he’ll be paid. The Colts could always extend Downs’ contract right now, but assuming they want to see more from him following a career-low 566 receiving yards in 2025, he’ll have to raise his level on the field. The 2023 third-round pick should have plenty of opportunities to do so since veteran Michael Pittman Jr., who led the Colts in catches in four of the past five years, was traded to the Pittsburgh Steelers in March. Downs now projects as the Colts’ clear No. 2 receiver behind the speedy and newly paid Alec Pierce.
Travis is taking over for veteran Braden Smith, who left the Colts to join the Houston Texans in free agency. Smith’s departure wasn’t surprising since his durability waned in recent years, yet he was still one of the Colts’ highest-paid offensive linemen. It’s logical for the Colts to have moved on to a younger and cheaper player in Travis, but Smith’s run with the Colts shouldn’t be quickly dismissed. He was an anchor on the right side for nearly a decade, and Travis is stepping into a huge role up front, especially when considering that Jones is coming off a torn Achilles tendon and needs pristine protection. If Travis, a 2025 fourth-round pick, can’t hold his own, he could lose his starting job quickly.
There’s only one number needed to describe Tuimoloau’s rookie season with the Colts: zero. The 2025 second-round pick started zero games and recorded zero sacks in his first year. In other words, he gave the Colts nothing. This year, Tuimoloau needs to do something, and he should have plenty of chances. Indianapolis said goodbye to veterans Kwity Paye, Samson Ebukam and Tyquan Lewis this offseason, and without signing another proven starting edge rusher in free agency to pair with Latu, it opens the door for Tuimoloau to earn his keep. If he still can’t get on the field under these circumstances, then it would be fair to label him as a missed pick.

title: Thoughts on the Vikings’ 46 defensive players ahead of training camp Ahead of training camp, we offer a thought on each player on the Vikings roster. We finish things off by breaking down the defense. Alec Lewis
summary:
With Jonathan Greenard departed, this will be an important training camp — and season — for edge rusher Dallas Turner. David Berding / Getty Images
The Minnesota Vikings staff returned to the TCO Performance Center this weekend. This week, the grind begins.
To preview the pandemonium, we’ve already compiled 45 thoughts on the team’s 45 offensive players . This time, we focus on the 46 defenders and special-teamers, including punter Brett Thorson, who is a member of the international pathway play
full_text:
With Jonathan Greenard departed, this will be an important training camp — and season — for edge rusher Dallas Turner. David Berding / Getty Images
The Minnesota Vikings staff returned to the TCO Performance Center this weekend. This week, the grind begins.
To preview the pandemonium, we’ve already compiled 45 thoughts on the team’s 45 offensive players . This time, we focus on the 46 defenders and special-teamers, including punter Brett Thorson, who is a member of the international pathway player program.
Note: Thoughts are in order of player jersey numbers.
Ivan Pace Jr., LB: His snaps decreased dramatically in 2025. He offers pass-rush juice, but his skills are better suited for special teams than an every-down role that requires exceptional coverage.
Isaiah Rodgers, CB: Would the Vikings’ improved cornerback depth allow special teams coordinator Matt Daniels to use him as a returner? Rodgers is dynamic enough.
Johnny Hekker, P: Accomplished but perhaps on the downturn. Hekker’s holding ability provides some security, but Thorson may push him.
Dwight McGlothern, CB: Faces an uphill battle to make the 53-man roster. Every year, McGlothern makes plays on the ball in training camp. He will need his best performance yet.
Byron Murphy Jr., CB: Looked explosive this spring. His drop in interceptions (from six in 2024 to two in 2025) frustrated him. Improved cornerback depth could allow him to play more nickel, giving the defense additional flexibility.
Jakobe Thomas, S: The Vikings were elated to land Thomas in the third round of the draft. His smarts, aggressiveness and blitzing ability should make him a viable option as a rookie.
Dallas Turner, Edge: The Vikings desperately need him to build off his progression in 2025, especially after losing Jonathan Greenard. The pass-rushing onus now falls on Turner.
Will Reichard, K: If you come at the king, you best not miss. Thinking about you, wires.
Charles Demmings, CB: Arrives with a megawatt smile and an electric personality. His athleticism pops, too. Should bring special teams explosiveness.
James Pierre, CB: An unheralded yet interesting signing. How Pierre performs against Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings in practice will be telling.
Jay Ward, S: Flashed at the end of last season. Ward is entering the final season of his rookie contract, and the Vikings need safeties to step up. Snaps are finally available.
Kahlef Hailassie, S: The Vikings were upset to lose him after his 2025 training camp when he landed with the Jaguars. He then returned and could vie for a spot on the back end.
Theo Jackson, S: Didn’t pop in his first season as a starter the way the Vikings hoped he would. A lack of safety depth could force him into a big role.
Tyreek Chappell, CB: An undersized, undrafted corner from Texas A&M who showed physicality at the catch point this spring.
Marcus Allen, CB: Has the name, but does he have the game? He, like Smith Vilbert, arrives from a similar defense at North Carolina with Bill Belichick at the helm.
Chaz Chambliss, Edge: Coaches eyed the former Georgia product as a versatile piece worthy of a roster spot last season. Chambliss can play on the edge and at linebacker. His work ethic inspires praise.
Zemaiah Vaughn, CB: Another developmental undrafted signing from last spring, Vaughn held his own last year in training camp. Displaying play strength could keep him on the 53-man roster.
Tavierre Thomas, S: If the Vikings load up at safety, Thomas becomes another option. He played almost all of the special teams snaps in 2025. Positional numbers could dictate his circumstances.
Da’Veawn Armstead, CB: Flew around noticeably this spring. This defensive staff tends to take a liking to a couple of undrafted players, which means the North Texas product has a shot.
Jacob Thomas, S: A sneaky undrafted signing out of James Madison, he got some reps with the second-teamers this spring. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores has an eye for safeties.
Jake Golday, LB: Began as a linebacker. Could get some reps at edge rusher. The Vikings loved his length, speed and anticipatory skills of this tone-setter.
Still unrefined, but his size, speed and ascending skill set are all encouraging.
Andrew DePaola, LS: Easily one of the coolest stories in the NFL . The man left college, stocked shelves at Best Buy, tended bar, then became a two-time first-team All-Pro.
Andrew Van Ginkel, Edge: Keeping the compliments to a minimum so that he doesn’t intercept them and ruin this exercise entirely.
Josh Metellus, S: Will he play in the deep half? Potential Hall of Famer Harrison Smith’s future remains up in the air. Metellus’ schematic understanding may mandate he calls signals from the back end.
Brett Thorson, P: There is a YouTube clip of his 75-yard punt against Tennessee. Thorson won the Ray Guy Award last season in college. Hekker must stay on high alert.
Jacob Roberts, LB: Talk about a journey here. Roberts began his college career at North Carolina A&T State University, transferred to Wake Forest and most recently played in the CFL for the Calgary Stampeders.
Cam’Ron Stewart, Edge: One of the easiest predictions is that the Vikings will add to their edge rusher room before the season. Stewart is an undrafted option from Temple.
Levi Drake Rodriguez, DT: One of his college coaches said that he used to show up to practice with different fruits tucked into his pockets. It no longer happens. Rodriguez, who attended Texas A&M-Commerce, still has some upside.
Blake Cashman, LB: His contract is set to void after the 2026 season, so it’s possible both he and the team could rework things this fall. Cashman has helped bring Flores’ defense to life since 2023.
Josh Ross, LB: Comes from the Mike Macdonald system in Baltimore and Seattle. Spent his time in 2025 on the Vikings’ practice squad. Familiarity matters.
Eric Wilson, LB: Unlocked more versatility for Flores. The Vikings played a majority of their snaps in 2025 in base defense (bigger bodies). Wilson’s range made this possible.
Arden Walker, Edge: An undrafted signing from Colorado, Walker will compete with a group of young off-ball linebackers for back-end roster and practice-squad spots.
Keli Lawson, LB: Another towering off-ball linebacker with range, Lawson played four years at Virginia Tech before a final season at UCF.
Bangally Kamara, LB: Criss-crossed the country in college, going from Pittsburgh to South Carolina to Kansas.
Jalen Redmond, DT: Evolved from an awesome story to an essential contributor. Considering the overwhelming youth on the Vikings’ defensive line, they need Redmond to make another leap.
Isaiahh Loudermilk, DT: Occupied a depth role for the Steelers from 2021 to 2025. Among the veteran interior defenders, he may be in pole position given his body type and ability to play several positions up front.

Smith Vilbert, DT: Raised eyebrows enough in a minicamp tryout to earn a shot. Vilbert’s exposure to Belichick’s defense in 2025 should help him transition to this system as a rookie.
Tyler Batty, Edge: Established his penchant to mix it up last year on special teams. Jawed with multiple opponents. Rugged and feisty.

full_text:
Second-year Patriots safety Craig Woodson has been a standout in the first two practices of training camp. Eric Canha / Imagn Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — It was a busy first weekend for the New England Patriots as training camp got underway. Owner Robert Kraft revealed that the team offered to make Christian Gonzalez the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history . Second-round pick Gabe Jacas finally signed his rookie contract. DeAndre Hopkins is roaming the sidelines while exploring a potential coaching role. And that doesn’t even get to the events of the first two practices on the fields outside Gillette Stadium.
The Patriots are still in the midst of the league’s mandated five-day ramp-up period, which means they can’t yet wear full pads. But there was still plenty to glean from the two weekend practices. Here’s what we’ve seen, heard and learned two days in.
It would be unwise to make much of the first two pad-free practices of the summer, but it’s worth noting that the Patriots defense has been better than the offense so far.
That’s usually how training camp goes. The passing offense needs to figure out its timing and get in a rhythm. Run blocking is tricky sans pads. So the defense usually looks good.
And that’s exactly what has happened so far. It doesn’t mean there’s any cause for concern with the offense, but the secondary, which is supposed to be the strength of the defense, has played exactly as the Patriots would have hoped.
Christian Gonzalez has fared well against A.J. Brown. Carlton Davis doesn’t look like he’s lost a step even with his 30th birthday on the horizon. And the two safeties are looking like they could be the strength of the unit with Craig Woodson shining next to Kevin Byard.
“Even though you do have dynamic players over there,” Byard said, “we’re a little bit ahead and making some plays. But when the pads come on and we get into training camp, I expect those guys to start making a lot more plays. But the defense has been having a lot of fun the first couple days.”
Part of the reason for the defense’s success is that Gonzalez has been a full participant even as his contract negotiations drag on. He’s part of the reason Brown has just one catch through two practices.
“The past couple days, I’ve really been seeing why he’s, in my opinion, the best corner in the league,” Byard said of Gonzalez. “He’s making a lot of plays and being sticky in coverage. … I feel really good about the secondary.”
Even with the defense getting the better of the offense the first two days, it’s been clear who the team’s best offensive player has been.
Kayshon Boutte hauled in deep passes on both Saturday and Sunday. That’s important not just because the offense leaned on explosive plays a year ago — and they will need to again. But it’s important because it was unclear how motivated Boutte was going to be entering camp.
He clearly has some frustration with his contract situation after skipping voluntary spring practices. Then, following his return in June, when asked about a potential extension, he said, “I wouldn’t mind being here.”
So some thought that maybe Boutte wouldn’t show up in top shape, or that he would try to force a trade. Instead, Boutte looks like he’s building off an impressive 2025 season (33 receptions for 551 yards and six touchdowns) when he was one of the league’s best deep-threat receivers.
“He’s made some really good catches (on) back-to-back days,” Byard said.
After a lengthy, drawn-out negotiation following an offseason surgery that occurred after the Patriots traded up in the second round to pick Gabe Jacas, the edge rusher became the final rookie of the 2026 draft class to sign his contract when he inked a four-year deal Sunday.
Still, it is not clear when Jacas will practice with the full roster for the first time. He was placed on the league’s active/non-football injury list. Jacas can’t practice while he has that designation, but he can be in team meetings.
His eventual presence on the field will be a needed boost for an edge rusher position that might be the weakness on the defense, especially while Harold Landry remains unable to practice because of a lingering knee injury.
Jacas opens training camp behind schedule after missing all of the team’s spring practices and not being present for meetings, but if he can catch up quickly, he could still play a meaningful role on this team.
A quick, aggressive pass rusher whose power and technique should translate well in the NFL.
Diehard Patriots fans recognized how well Woodson played as a rookie last season, especially in the playoffs. But Woodson may earn more national recognition if he keeps playing like this.
Drake Maye targeted Brown on a crossing pass during Saturday’s practice, but the throw was a bit high and went off Brown’s fingers. Woodson made an impressive adjustment to go from covering Brown to nabbing the first interception of training camp.
Byard may be the more recognizable name among the safeties after leading the NFL in interceptions a year ago, but Woodson looks like he’s picking up right where he left off last season.

title: Ranking the Giants' 6 most indispensable players: Who can N.Y. least afford to lose? Quarterback Jaxson Dart made the list, but he's not No. 1. Should he be? Charlotte Carroll
summary:
Is left tackle Andrew Thomas the most indispensable player on the New York Giants' roster? Al Bello / Getty Images
After a transformative offseason, a new era of New York Giants football kicks off this week as the team heads to West Virginia to begin training camp.
Amid the coaching changes and roster turnover, however, there will still be plenty of familiar faces tasked with getting this team back on the path to success. Some, of course, will play a more critical role than others, which got me
full_text:
Is left tackle Andrew Thomas the most indispensable player on the New York Giants' roster? Al Bello / Getty Images
After a transformative offseason, a new era of New York Giants football kicks off this week as the team heads to West Virginia to begin training camp.
Amid the coaching changes and roster turnover, however, there will still be plenty of familiar faces tasked with getting this team back on the path to success. Some, of course, will play a more critical role than others, which got me thinking: Which players can the Giants least afford to lose right now?
A few of my colleagues around The Athletic have undertaken similar exercises, and I thought it would be fun to try it out ahead of training camp, where, unfortunately, injuries will start to pile up.
The names on this list probably won’t surprise you, but the rankings might. When compiling my list, I considered more than pure talent, though that’s obviously a big factor. I also considered the depth behind these players, their leadership qualities and the schematic changes required if any of these players were forced to miss a significant period of time.
Let’s examine the six most indispensable Giants this season:
You don’t need to use your imagination to think about what the Giants’ offense looks like without Thomas. Giants fans have gotten a few too many looks at that unfortunate scenario in recent years. Thomas missed seven games in 2023, the same season in which the team surrendered the second-most sacks in NFL history (85). In 2024, he played just six games before suffering a Lisfranc injury, and the Giants yielded 48 sacks, the 11th-most in the NFL. From 2024-25, the Giants’ offense scored 10.9 points per game without Thomas on the field, versus 13.5 points per game when he was on the field, according to TruMedia.
He’s a critical cog in the offense, and if he were to miss time, the Giants would have to turn to 2025 fifth-rounder Marcus Mbow. While Mbow has shown talent, Thomas’ talent and experience are nearly impossible to replace. As one of the longest-tenured Giants, Thomas is a stalwart and an anchoring presence for an offense that desperately needs him to stay healthy.
Nabers is another player whose absence severely impacts the offense, as fans found out last season when he missed 13 games with ACL and meniscus tears. You don’t need a reminder of how grim things got for the passing offense without Nabers on the field, but I’ll give one anyway: From the time Nabers missed his first game (Week 5), until the end of the season, the Giants’ offense finished in the bottom half of the league in passing yards, passing touchdowns and completion rate. Giants receivers, meanwhile, finished seventh in drops (19) in that span.
Despite learning what life is like without Nabers, the Giants didn’t really try to insulate themselves in case he again misses significant time. Last season’s leading receiver, Wan’Dale Robinson, departed in free agency. To replace him, the Giants added cheap veteran Darnell Mooney, along with ex-Ravens tight end Isaiah Likely. The team then spent a third-round pick on Malachi Fields before signing veterans Odell Beckham Jr., JuJu Smith-Schuster and Braxton Berrios to low-cost deals in the spring.
While there are plenty of pieces for the coaching staff to work with, the depth chart doesn’t appear to be flush with playmakers outside of Nabers. The 22-year-old is New York’s one proven dynamic weapon who can change the way defenses prepare for the Giants’ offense. Without him, the Giants are likely to struggle to move the ball through the air.
You might have expected to see Dart higher on this list, but the truth is the young QB is only going into his second year, and we don’t really know how good he can be. The 23-year-old has thrown just 339 passes at the NFL level, and while he looked good in his 14 games last season, it’s still too early to know just how much room he has to grow.
Still, Dart has quickly emerged as one of the team’s leaders, and his presence is a big reason coach John Harbaugh is in New York, too.
The other reason Dart fell to No. 3 here is that he has a high-quality backup in Jameis Winston, who might be one of the best QB2s in the league. If Dart were to miss time, the Giants offense would obviously lose something, but Winston is more than capable of leading New York to victories. That said, if Dart takes another big step in his development this year, he will have a compelling case for the top spot next season.
Jermaine Eluemunor blossomed into a reliable right tackle for the Giants last year, which earned him a three-year, $39 million contract. I also considered Likely, whom the Giants signed to a three-year, $40 million contract in free agency. However, we’ve yet to see him play a meaningful snap in a Giants uniform, so it would be hard to justify ranking him ahead of anyone on this list.
Not only is Burns a top-tier pass rusher who tallied an NFC-best 16.5 sacks last season, but he’s also a highly respected veteran within the Giants locker room. Just look at the turnout of teammates who showed up for his charity softball game this spring. So yes, he might be part of one of the best position rooms on the team , which hurts his case for being the most indispensable, but his presence as the face of the defense — especially with Dexter Lawrence out of town — isn’t as easily replaceable.
Quite the team show of support for Brian Burns softball game today.
Spot the #giants pic.twitter.com/5uArtLBPsg
— Charlotte Carroll (@charlottecrrll) May 30, 2026
Unexpected choice? Maybe, but hear me out. You already knew the Giants’ defensive line depth was thin before the Dexter Lawrence trade. Then Roy Robertson-Harris tore his Achilles, and while he isn’t on injured reserve, he’s going to miss significant time this year. So, that leaves Reader, a post-draft free agent acquisition, as the focal point of the Giants’ run-stopping unit. Stopping the run has been a major problem for the Giants, even with Lawrence in the fold. From 2024-25, the Giants have surrendered a league-high 4.9 yards per carry.
If Reader, now 32, and his teammates can’t halt opposing teams’ rushing attacks, then the Giants’ top asset, its fearsome pass rush, will be nullified. And if Reader were to miss time, there isn’t much high-quality depth behind him.
This is a bit more of a projection, but if the defense is going to be better than average in 2026, it will likely be because Carter developed into a game-wrecker in his second season. He was drafted No. 3 to be a difference-maker, and we saw flashes of that last season. Carter led the league in quick pressures with 48, according to Next Gen Stats, and tallied a team-high 66 total pressures to go along with four sacks, per TruMedia. With a secondary facing questions, generating more quick pressure would help the defensive backs not have to cover for too long. Carter has the talent to make the entire defense better, which is why he made this list.
The Giants need Paulson Adebo to be a stalwart at CB1, given the questions surrounding the No. 2 spot. The cornerback position is probably the one with the biggest position battle, so feeling good about Adebo up top is the ideal scenario for the Giants.
